label: Chinchilla's 20-tokens-per-parameter ratio is universally optimal
description:
Chinchilla (Hoffmann et al. 2022) was a watershed result: at the time, frontier models were under-trained, and the new optimal allocation suggested ~20 tokens per parameter. The ratio became gospel quickly. It's not.

Three reasons the ratio is regime-specific:

**1. The exponents depend on the LR schedule.** Chinchilla used cosine LR decay to the end of training. Kaplan (the earlier paper) used constant LR. The two papers got *different* optimal ratios partly because the LR schedule changes how loss scales with data. If you're using a different schedule (linear decay, plateau, multi-stage), the law's exponents shift.

**2. The ratio is for *training-only* compute.** Chinchilla optimizes the compute to reach a given loss. It doesn't account for inference cost. If you're going to serve a model T times, the over-training tradeoff changes: a smaller, over-trained model is cheaper to serve. LLaMA-3 8B trained on 15T tokens (~1900 tokens/param) is *deliberately* over-trained relative to Chinchilla because the inference economics favor it.

**3. Data quality matters.** The ratio assumes uniform-quality tokens. Heavily filtered data shifts the curve down — same nominal D, lower loss. The 'effective D' depends on your data pipeline.

Use 20:1 as a starting heuristic when training a model only for one-time evaluation. For models you'll serve in production, expect to over-train (50:1, 100:1, or more). Re-fit the law for your specific recipe before committing big compute.
probeQuestions: Why did Kaplan's 2020 paper conclude '~2 tokens per parameter' while Chinchilla concluded '~20 tokens per parameter'?
If you're going to serve a model 1 trillion times after training, should you use the Chinchilla ratio?
correctionPromptTemplate: The learner thinks Chinchilla's 20:1 ratio is a universal constant. Walk through: the exponents depend on the LR schedule (Kaplan vs Chinchilla disagreed largely because of this); the ratio is training-only optimal, not inference-amortized optimal; data quality changes the effective D. Modern over-training (LLaMA-3 at 1900:1) is the response to inference economics. Ask first — 'if 20:1 were universal, why does Meta train LLaMA-3 at much higher ratios?'
